Consult Summary:
- Acute onset left upper limb immobility with left facial tingling, dysphagia and speech difficulty that began approximately one hour prior to call.
- Provider concerned for possible acute stroke; ambulance dispatched to patient’s home and patient instructed to await transfer to hospital for emergency assessment.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute focal neurological deficit — suspected stroke
- Presentation: sudden inability to move left arm beginning ~1 hour before the consultation; no associated pain, no hand discoloration, hand not cold.
- Associated symptoms: tingling on the left side of the face since onset, difficulty swallowing when drinking, speech described as slower and more difficult.
- Systems review / pertinent negatives: no left leg symptoms reported; no facial asymmetry observed by patient; no acute chest pain or other symptoms documented.
- Examination findings (telephone report): persistent left arm weakness (unable to move), left facial tingling, progressive speech difficulty.
- Specialist/allied review and differential: ambulance en route for hospital transfer; doctor expressed concern for stroke and stated stroke team in A&E will assess for possible acute stroke treatment.

Issue 2: Chronic medical conditions — Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension
- History: patient reports type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.
- Medications: patient reports taking metformin, losartan and amlodipine (doses/routes/frequencies not documented).
- Relevance: these conditions are vascular risk factors pertinent to current presentation.

Issue 3: Social situation and immediate safety
- Living situation: normally lives alone; currently alone at home during acute event.
- Immediate safety plan: advised to leave front door unlocked and sit in hallway to facilitate ambulance access; ambulance dispatched and clinician remained on line until arrival.
- Social history relevant to risk: ex-smoker; alcohol: beers — “a few drinks over the weekend” and “a couple more during the week.”

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Losartan — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Amlodipine — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Penicillin.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Hypertension.

Social History:
- Lives alone.
- Former smoker (no quantity/timing documented).
- Alcohol: beers; described as a few on weekends and a couple during the week.
- Family history: father with heart disease (no further detail).

Preventative History:
- No preventative care items (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) were mentioned in the consult.

Physical Examination:
- No formal vital signs or in-person examination documented.
- Telephone-reported findings: inability to move left arm, left facial tingling, worsening speech difficulty; no hand discoloration, hand not cold.
- Clinician unable to visualize patient during consult (telephone appointment).

Plan:
- Immediate: ambulance dispatched to patient’s home for transfer to local A&E; remain at home, keep front door unlocked and sit in hallway for access.
- Hospital: A&E assessment with stroke team review and emergency management as indicated (ambulance/hospital to determine specific interventions).
- Clinician action: doctor arranged ambulance and remained on the line until ambulance arrival.
- Follow-up: not specified in the transcript — hospital-based follow-up to be determined after assessment.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation), blood glucose, exact time of symptom onset/last known well (patient stated ~1 hour but exact clock time not recorded), neurological examination details (facial asymmetry, limb power grading, NIHSS), medication doses/routes/frequencies, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, baseline functional status, advance directives.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: none identified.
- Transcript quality comment: audio conversational with some pauses but clinically relevant information clearly conveyed; telephone limitation prevented visual examination.
